fetched_contents.text: China’s Property Rebalancing: The Long Road to a New Development Model China’s property slump, now in its fifth year, has shown few signs of abating. Since the start of the decade, real estate investment has plunged nearly 44%, driven by a steeper collapse in home sales (figure 1). Official data indicate average new home prices have fallen roughly 20% from their 2021 peak, though actual declines are likely double that figure once one accounts for government limits on how steeply developers can officially discount prices.1 As housing remains the primary store of household wealth in China, declining property values have encouraged precautionary savings and dampened consumption. Collapsing sales ravaged developer cash flow, forcing defensive deleveraging and dragging down investment across construction-related industries. Shrinking land-sales revenue has exacerbated local government debt pressures and constrained public spending.2 Beijing’s response has remained cautious, focused on containing financial risks. Authorities have gradually dismantled the “Three Red Lines” financing restrictions, launched whitelist lending programs for unfinished projects, lowered mortgage costs, and pushed cities to abandon home-purchase restrictions.3 None of these measures have been sufficient to reverse the persistent deterioration in homebuyer sentiment. A central paradox in Beijing’s housing strategy is the disconnect between assertive top-level rhetoric — calls to “halt the decline and restore stability” (止跌回稳) since September 2024 — and a markedly restrained policy playbook. That restraint reflects a competing long-term agenda, officially framed as the "new property development model" (房地产发展新模式), which limits the scope and intensity of market stabilization.4 After the July 2023 Politburo meeting, Xi Jinping’s signature slogan “housing is for living in, not for speculation” all but vanished from high-level messaging.5 Markets interpreted this as a signal that Beijing’s deleveraging campaign had given way to short-term stimulus. The reality is more nuanced: the core tenets of the anti-speculation drive had been repackaged into the “new development model” — a framework officially debuted at the Central Economic Work Conference (CEWC) in late 2022 and now the overarching directive for the property sector in the 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP).6 The new model is unfolding across three dimensions. First, from primary growth driver to macroeconomic anchor. Real estate has long occupied an outsized role in China’s economic activity, although its weight has declined in recent years. In the decade before the housing downturn began, property investment consistently accounted for 25% to 30% of total fixed-asset investment; after peaking in 2020, that share had fallen to 16.9% by 2025 (figure 2). China’s economic rebalancing now requires credit and crucial resources to be further redirected toward advanced manufacturing and future industries — the foundations of “new quality productive forces.” Under the new model, real estate is no longer expected to serve as a primary engine of growth, but rather to sustain baseline demand across construction, upstream industrial inputs, and employment.7 Second, from speculative investment vehicle to a housing model more centered on livability and affordability. Property price inflation had delivered high returns to urban households but vastly outpaced income growth over the past two decades, producing price-to-income ratios exceeding 20–30x in major cities.8 The new development model seeks to shift housing away from its role as a primary wealth accumulation vehicle and toward its social function as shelter, by incrementally increasing the share of affordable housing in new supply and steering the market toward greater price stability, rather than another cycle of rapid appreciation and painful correction.9 Third, from land-sale dependency to fiscally sustainable local governance. China’s local governments have been selling land-use rights to cover expenditure gaps and supplement infrastructure funding. The new development model demands a transition away from one-off fiscal windfalls toward more sustainable revenue sources. Fiscal arrangements, including through a broader local tax base, reforms to central-local revenue sharing, and, over the longer term, new recurrent sources of local revenue, such as a property tax. Operationalizing the new development model amid a deep downturn exposes at least four serious internal contradictions. China’s overarching economic rebalancing strategy demands that the property sector shrink to free up resources for emerging, higher-value industries. But the depth and duration of the housing downturn have clearly exceeded policymakers’ expectations. The prolonged demand adjustment has pushed many developers into severe cash-flow stress, while the drag on growth, upstream and downstream industries, and employment has become far larger than Beijing appears willing to tolerate. As a result, policymakers have come to face a dual mandate: they still want to reduce the economy’s long-standing dependence on property, but they also feel increasingly compelled to arrest the downturn before its macroeconomic spillovers become too damaging.10 The evolution of Central Economic Work Conference (CEWC) language reflects this contradiction with increasing clarity. From 2019 to 2021, the emphasis remained on market stability, while the reform message was still framed in largely disciplinary terms through the slogan that “housing is for living in, not for speculation.” In 2022, amid deepening stress in the sector, the language shifted from curbing speculation to ensuring “stable development” and a “smooth transition” to a new development model. Despite a 6% year-on-year rise in fossil gas consumption, CO2 emissions from the power sector, China’s largest emitter, fell by 3% overall. This depends largely on the future trajectory of coal use in sectors, such as chemicals and heating, as well as trends in non-CO2 emissions. China’s rapid renewables rollout is the main driver for China’s decarbonisation. By the end of June 2025, total renewable capacity, including hydropower, reached 2,159 GW, representing nearly 60% of the country’s total power generation capacity. fetched_contents.text: rise of sustainable finance in China: ESG funds and regulation | Capital Markets Law Journal Abstract This article examines the emerging ecosystem of ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) funds in China, focusing on their classification, regulation, and policy context. It presents a taxonomy of ESG funds in the Chinese market, including public, private, government-guided, and Public–Private Partnership (PPP) funds. It analyses China’s distinctive policy-driven transformation model on ESG, emphasizing its top-down design and the pivotal role of State-owned Enterprises (SOEs), and the use of phased policy implementation. Compared to the European Union’s sophisticated disclosure and taxonomy regime, China requires clearer legal definitions, mandatory reporting mechanisms, and a unified classification system on ESG funds. The crucial future task involves balancing government intervention with market forces to ensure capital is channelled into the real economy’s green transformation. This will be essential for establishing an internationally competitive sustainable finance framework and ensuring capital genuinely supports industrial upgrading and sustainable development. Issue Section: Article > Special Issue: Sustainable Investment Management in a Changing World Collection: Oxford Law Pro 1. Introduction The integration of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles into investment strategies has gained significant traction in China in recent years. Chinese policymakers and financial institutions have increasingly acknowledged that mobilizing capital in alignment with ESG objectives can play a critical role in advancing national priorities, including the ‘dual carbon’ targets of peaking carbon emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060, promised by President Xi Jinping during the general debate of the 75th session of the United Nations General Assembly in 2020.1 The growth of ESG-focused, green or sustainable-themed investment funds in China thus reflects both an internal policy imperative to promote green finance and an external response to international sustainability standards. The origins of the ESG fund landscape in China can be traced to 2011, when the Industrial Bank of China launched the Xingquan Green Investment Equity Securities Investment Fund, the country’s first fund dedicated to investments in energy-saving, new-energy, and environmental-protection enterprises. In October of the same year, the State Council issued the Opinions of the State Council on Strengthening Major Environmental Protection Work, which expressly provided the policy goal to ‘encourage the establishment of various development funds for the environmental protection industry to broaden its financing avenues’,2 thereby furnishing policy support for the creation of such funds.3 Building on this early momentum, the People’s Bank of China, the Ministry of Finance, and other competent authorities jointly issued the Guidelines for Establishing the Green Financial System in 2016, which explicitly mandated to ‘support the establishment of all types of green development funds and implement market-oriented operations’ and ‘encourage all types of green development funds to support the relevant programs operated in the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) mode’,4 among other measures.5 These successive policy instruments collectively signalled a clear and sustained commitment at the central level to fostering the growth of green investment vehicles.6 The development of green financial instruments in China has followed a phased and sequential trajectory. In the early stages, policy and regulatory efforts were primarily concentrated on green credit7 and green bonds.8 Within this context, green industrial funds, especially those closely aligned with industrial policy and established under government guidance or participation, began to emerge as important vehicles for promoting specific green sectors. Notably, the establishment of such funds was most active between 2014 and 2016.9 As market mechanisms matured and awareness of ESG principles increased, ESG-themed publicly offered funds10 and market-driven green private equity (PE) and venture capital (VC) funds began to expand rapidly. This trend accelerated significantly following the introduction of China’s ‘dual carbon’ goals in 2020, which triggered substantial growth in both the number and scale of ESG publicly offered funds. By 2022, the assets under the management of ESG publicly offered funds continued to grow steadily. This shift from policy-driven, government-led financial tools to a more diversified and market-oriented product landscape has fundamentally shaped the current structure of China’s ESG fund market. Despite recent progress, ESG funds remain underdeveloped within China’s broader green finance policy framework.11 China’s green finance sector has established a prominent global position and exhibits substantial potential for further development. Recent data indicate that, by the end of 2024, the outstanding balance of green loans in China reached RMB 36.6 trillion.12 Furthermore, the domestic green bond market saw significant activity in 2023, with issuance volume surpassing RMB 940 billion.13 By the end of 2024, the cumulative issuance of green bonds had exceeded RMB 4.1 trillion.14 As of 2024, debt financing instruments (primarily green credit and green bonds) accounted for as much as 97 per cent of total green finance, while equity financing comprised less than 3 per cent.15 This structural imbalance is likely to slow progress towards achieving the ‘dual carbon’ objectives. Abstract Urban residential land supply is both driven by and significantly influences urbanisation processes, the optimisation of which are necessary to address housing issues. At present, China's urban housing system has three major problems, namely a shortage of affordable housing, rapidly increasing prices for regular commodity housing, and an under-supply, relative to market demands, of high-end commodity housing, calling into question the effectiveness of existing land supply policies. The model demonstrates how reformation of the residential land supply system through improvements to the elasticity of residential land supply, optimisation of land supply for affordable housing, deregulation of land supply for and taxation of high-end commodity housing will significantly ease housing stress within Chinese cities. The real estate industry’s sustainable development is being driven by a combination of regulatory pressure, market behavior, and technical operational improvements, but the evidence base here is relatively thin and partially indirect.

On regulatory and policy levers, the most directly relevant evidence shows a strong shift toward green building and land-use planning. The 14th Five-Year Plan of China’s Green Buildings was issued in March 2022 and put forward higher requirements for high-quality development of green buildings [N1-R3]. By 2025, all new urban buildings must comply with green building standards, and the total floor area of newly constructed nearly zero energy buildings is to be expanded [N1-R5]. A separate climate-action-source excerpt also indicates that China’s sectoral 14th Five-Year Plans set out mitigation measures for a post-coal transition and are on track to meet energy-sector targets, with renewables continuing to dominate deployment [N1-F2]. In addition, the broader urban-planning context shows that Chinese authorities have issued various policies and regulations on land use, environmental management, and related areas in response to the pandemic [N1-R2]. Taken together, these sources support a policy environment in which green building standards and land-use rules are central regulatory levers for sustainability [N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-R2].

On market and investor behavior, the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The green-finance literature points to a market-driven ecosystem in which ESG funds and sustainable finance are becoming prominent, with a taxonomy of ESG funds including public, private, government-guided, and PPP funds [N2-F3]. China’s green finance market is described as at a nascent stage but well poised for rapid growth, supported by the steady development of its green finance system [N2-R2]. Green bonds and other instruments are increasingly important, with debt financing instruments such as green credit and green bonds accounting for as much as 97 percent of total green finance as of 2024 [N2-R1]. The evidence also notes that regulators are tightening expectations on use-of-proceeds, impact indicators, and external review for labelled green and sustainability bonds [N2-R3]. This suggests that market participants are being incentivized to align with ESG standards and green finance mechanisms, but the evidence does not provide detailed industry behavior data beyond the existence of these financial tools [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

On technical and operational drivers, the evidence emphasizes energy efficiency and decarbonization but does not provide a granular breakdown of material use. The climate-action-source excerpt notes that renewables capacity has reached 2,159 GW by the end of June 2025, representing nearly 60% of total power generation capacity, with renewables supplying almost 40% of power generation in H1 2025 [N1-F2]. It also indicates that China’s rapid renewables rollout is the main driver of decarbonisation, while the power sector remains the country’s largest emitter [N1-F2]. The same source notes that the NDRC’s new draft implementation measures mark a shift from supply-side incentives to demand-side obligations, introducing a mandatory minimum proportion target of renewable energy consumption [N1-F2]. This points to operational efficiency and energy-system restructuring as key technical drivers, but it does not explicitly detail material-use improvements or other operational efficiency levers [N1-F2]. The comparative policy-context evidence also suggests that China uses a planning-driven model focused on national goals and technical standards, implying that technical standards and planning are part of the broader sustainability toolkit [N4-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: sustainable development in the real estate industry is being pushed by green building standards, renewable-energy transition policy, land-use regulation, and a growing green finance market [N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the evidence is uneven on market behavior and technical operational details, so some conclusions must be stated cautiously [N1-F2][N4-R1].

The state is likely to support real estate development over the next decade through a combination of policy tools, financial and capital mechanisms, and land/housing/urban planning signals, but the evidence points to a cautious and transitional framework rather than a single unified blueprint.

On policy tools, the most directly relevant evidence shows a shift from stabilization to structural rebalancing. China’s property slump has persisted for five years, and Beijing’s response has remained cautious, focusing on containing financial risks rather than aggressive stimulus [N1-F1]. Authorities have gradually dismantled the “Three Red Lines” financing restrictions, launched whitelist lending programs for unfinished projects, lowered mortgage costs, and pushed cities to abandon home-purchase restrictions [N1-F1]. The “new property development model” is described as the overarching directive for the property sector in the 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP), and it unfolds across three dimensions: from primary growth driver to macroeconomic anchor, from speculative investment vehicle to housing centered on livability and affordability, and from land-sale dependency to fiscally sustainable local governance [N1-F1]. This indicates that the government is likely to use policy tools that combine financial easing, credit support, affordability measures, and fiscal governance reform [N1-F1]. The climate-action-source excerpt also reinforces that China’s current policies scenario projects emissions around 14.6–15.3 GtCO2e in 2030, and it highlights the importance of renewable energy capacity, renewable energy consumption targets, and coal reduction [N1-F2]. Taken together, the policy toolkit appears to be centered on stabilization, affordability, fiscal sustainability, and decarbonization [N1-F1][N1-F2].

On financial and capital support mechanisms, the evidence shows a strong role for green finance and ESG capital, with debt financing instruments such as green credit and green bonds accounting for as much as 97 percent of total green finance as of 2024 [N2-R1]. China’s green finance market is described as nascent but well poised for rapid growth, supported by the steady development of its green finance system [N2-R2]. The ESG-finance source notes that ESG funds are increasingly important, including public, private, government-guided, and PPP funds, and that the market has shifted from policy-driven, government-led tools to a more diversified and market-oriented product landscape [N2-F3]. It also highlights that the growth of ESG funds reflects both an internal policy imperative and an external response to international sustainability standards [N2-F3]. The evidence further notes that green bonds and other instruments are essential for meeting environmental goals, and that regulators are tightening expectations on use-of-proceeds, impact indicators, and external review [N2-R3]. These sources support a capital-support environment in which green credit, green bonds, ESG funds, and broader green finance mechanisms are the main channels through which the state can support sustainable development [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F3][N2-R3].

On land, housing, and urban planning signals, the evidence points to a mixed but reform-oriented direction. China’s urban-planning context shows that authorities have issued various policies and regulations on land use, environmental management, and related areas in response to the pandemic [N1-R2]. The housing-rebalancing source notes that land-use rights revenue dropped by over 50% between 2021 and 2025, and that local governments face financial obligations to subsidize housing [N1-R1]. It also indicates that the new development model demands a transition away from one-off fiscal windfalls toward more sustainable revenue sources, including a broader local tax base, reforms to central-local revenue sharing, and, over the longer term, new recurrent sources of local revenue such as a property tax [N1-F1]. The land-supply-reform literature suggests that supply-side structural reform of the land market can help integrate land, capital, and labor factors and increase effective supply [N5-R4]. It also notes that improving the efficiency of the supply of developable land and real estate is more effective than simply increasing allocations of land for residential development [N5-R5]. Taken together, the urban planning and land signals suggest a move toward more sustainable fiscal arrangements, more efficient land-use planning, and greater integration of land, capital, and labor [N1-R2][N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a policy-support framework in which the state will likely use financial easing, green finance, ESG capital, affordability measures, fiscal governance reform, land-use regulation, and supply-side land reform to support real estate development [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F3][N2-R3][N1-R2][N1-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The most important signal is that the government is no longer treating real estate as a primary growth engine, but as a baseline demand anchor for construction, upstream inputs, and employment [N1-F1]. That makes the future support package more structural than cyclical [N1-F1].

The future of China’s real estate industry faces significant risks and structural changes, but the evidence is strongest on supply-side bottlenecks and less direct on demand-side demographic trends. It also points to regulatory risks and changing development models driven by urbanization slowdown and ESG demands.

On demographic and demand-side pressures, the evidence is limited and indirect. The strongest relevant source is the housing-rebalancing report, which notes that China’s property downturn has lasted five years and that declining property values have encouraged precautionary savings and dampened consumption [N1-F1]. It also states that housing remains the primary store of household wealth in China, and that declining property values have created a paradox between assertive top-level rhetoric and a restrained policy playbook [N1-F1]. This suggests that demand-side pressures are real and persistent, but the source does not provide a detailed demographic outlook for the next decade. The urbanization and land-supply literature also notes that urban populations are expected to expand by 255 million by 2050, which intensifies urban housing shortfalls [N5-F4]. However, this is presented as a background socioeconomic condition rather than a near-term demand-side constraint [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that demand-side pressures will remain a concern, especially through affordability and consumption-side effects, but it does not provide a robust, decade-specific demographic forecast [N1-F1][N5-F4].

On regulatory and enforcement risks in sustainability implementation, the evidence is mixed. On one hand, the green-finance literature indicates that regulators are tightening expectations on use-of-proceeds, impact indicators, and external review for labelled green and sustainability bonds [N2-R3]. This suggests that implementation risks are being addressed through stricter oversight. On the other hand, the climate-action-source excerpt notes that China’s current policies scenario are rated as “Insufficient” when compared to their fair-share contribution to climate change mitigation [N1-F2]. It also notes that China’s climate policies and action need substantial improvements to be consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C, and that if all countries followed China’s approach, warming would reach over 2°C and up to 3°C [N1-F2]. This implies that enforcement risks and policy gaps may persist if China cannot accelerate its climate transition. The housing-rebalancing source also indicates that local governments have been selling land-use rights to cover expenditure gaps and supplement infrastructure funding, and that the new development model demands a transition away from one-off fiscal windfalls toward more sustainable revenue sources [N1-F1]. While this is more about fiscal governance than direct sustainability enforcement, it still reflects the risk that weak implementation of new policy frameworks can undermine sustainability goals [N1-F1][N1-F2].

On how urbanization slowdown and ESG demands will change development models, the evidence points to a structural shift toward affordability, livability, and decarbonization. The new property development model is described as shifting housing away from its role as a primary wealth accumulation vehicle toward its social function as shelter, by incrementally increasing the share of affordable housing in new supply and steering the market toward greater price stability [N1-F1]. The land-supply-reform literature argues that current Chinese national government policies are insufficient to resolve urban housing shortfalls, that demand for affordable housing far outstrips supply, and that reforms should integrate housing provision across affordable and commodity sectors [N5-F4]. It also suggests that deregulation of land supply for and taxation of high-end commodity housing can ease housing stress [N5-F4]. At the same time, the energy-transition excerpt shows that China’s rapid renewables rollout is the main driver of decarbonisation and that the NDRC’s draft implementation measures are shifting from supply-side incentives to demand-side obligations [N1-F2]. This indicates that future development models will be more focused on sustainable energy systems, affordable housing, and integrated land-use planning rather than on speculative price growth [N1-F1][N5-F4][N1-F2]. The comparative policy-context evidence also notes that China uses a planning-driven model focused on national goals and technical standards, which is consistent with a more controlled, technical, and long-term development model [N4-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a conclusion that future risks include persistent affordability and fiscal constraints, potential enforcement gaps in sustainability implementation, and the possibility that regulatory looseness may not be sufficient to stabilize demand [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. The structural change direction is clear: development models are likely to become more affordable, more livability-centered, and more aligned with ESG and decarbonization requirements [N1-F1][N5-F4][N1-F2].

# Integrated final answer: drivers and future policy direction for sustainable real estate development

## 1) What drives sustainable development in the real estate industry?

The real estate industry’s sustainable development is being driven by a combination of **regulatory and policy levers, market and investor behavior, and technical and operational improvements**. However, the evidence is uneven: it is strongest on policy and regulatory forces, less direct on market behavior, and thinner on granular technical operational details.

### 1.1 Regulatory and policy levers

The most direct evidence points to green building standards and land-use planning. By 2025, **all new urban buildings must comply with green building standards**, and the **14th Five-Year Plan of China’s Green Buildings** raised requirements for high-quality development [N1-R3][N1-R5]. A broader policy context also shows that Chinese authorities have issued various policies and regulations on **land use, environmental management, and related areas** in response to the pandemic [N1-R2]. These sources indicate that sustainability in real estate is being driven by national standards and regulatory oversight.

At the same time, China’s climate policy context reinforces the role of broader environmental and energy transition goals. China’s sectoral 14th Five-Year Plans set out mitigation measures for a post-coal transition and are on track to meet energy-sector targets, while **renewables continue to dominate deployment** [N1-F2]. The climate-action source also notes that the **NDRC’s new draft implementation measures** mark a shift from supply-side incentives to demand-side obligations, introducing a mandatory minimum proportion target of renewable energy consumption [N1-F2]. This suggests that sustainability is being reinforced not only through building codes but also through energy-system restructuring.

### 1.2 Market and investor behavior

The market side is less directly evidenced, but the evidence is suggestive. The green-finance literature points to a market-driven ecosystem in which **ESG funds and sustainable finance** are becoming prominent. China’s green finance market is described as **nascent but well poised for rapid growth**, supported by the steady development of its green finance system [N2-R2]. Green bonds and other instruments are increasingly important, with **debt financing instruments such as green credit and green bonds accounting for as much as 97 percent of total green finance as of 2024** [N2-R1]. The evidence also notes that **regulators are tightening expectations on use-of-proceeds, impact indicators, and external review for labelled green and sustainability bonds** [N2-R3]. This suggests that market participants are being incentivized to align with ESG standards and green finance mechanisms, even if the sources do not provide detailed industry behavior data.

### 1.3 Technical and operational drivers

The technical side is clearer in terms of energy efficiency and decarbonization than in material-use details. The climate-action source indicates that **renewables capacity has reached 2,159 GW by the end of June 2025**, representing nearly **60% of total power generation capacity**, with renewables supplying almost **40% of power generation** in H1 2025 [N1-F2]. It also states that the **rapid renewables rollout is the main driver of decarbonisation**, while the **power sector remains the country’s largest emitter** [N1-F2]. The comparative policy-context evidence further notes that China uses a **planning-driven model focused on national goals and technical standards**, implying that technical standards and planning are part of the broader sustainability toolkit [N4-R1].

In short, the main drivers are:  
- **green building standards and land-use regulation** [N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-R2];  
- **ESG finance and green bonds** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3];  
- **renewables, energy-system restructuring, and decarbonization** [N1-F2];  
- **technical standards and planning** [N4-R1].

## 2) How the state will support real estate development over the next decade

The evidence points to a cautious and transitional policy framework: the state is likely to use **policy tools, financial and capital mechanisms, and land/housing/urban planning signals**, but the emphasis is on **stabilization, affordability, fiscal sustainability, and structural rebalancing** rather than aggressive stimulus.

### 2.1 Policy tools

The housing-rebalancing report shows that China’s property slump has lasted five years, and Beijing’s response has remained cautious, focusing on containing financial risks rather than aggressive stimulus [N1-F1]. Authorities have gradually dismantled the “Three Red Lines” financing restrictions, launched **whitelist lending programs for unfinished projects**, lowered mortgage costs, and pushed cities to abandon home-purchase restrictions [N1-F1]. The **new property development model** is the overarching directive for the property sector in the 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP), and it unfolds across three dimensions:  
- from **primary growth driver to macroeconomic anchor**,  
- from **speculative investment vehicle to housing centered on livability and affordability**,  
- from **land-sale dependency to fiscally sustainable local governance** [N1-F1].

This indicates that the government is likely to use policy tools that combine **financial easing, credit support, affordability measures, and fiscal governance reform** [N1-F1].

### 2.2 Financial and capital support mechanisms

The financial side is strong on green finance and ESG capital. Green credit and green bonds account for **as much as 97 percent of total green finance as of 2024** [N2-R1]. China’s green finance market is described as **nascent but well poised for rapid growth**, supported by the steady development of its green finance system [N2-R2]. The ESG-finance source notes that **ESG funds** are increasingly important, including public, private, government-guided, and PPP funds, and that the market has shifted from policy-driven, government-led tools to a more **diversified and market-oriented product landscape** [N2-F3]. It also emphasizes that the growth of ESG funds reflects both an **internal policy imperative** and an **external response to international sustainability standards** [N2-F3].

The evidence also indicates that **regulators are tightening expectations on use-of-proceeds, impact indicators, and external review for labelled green and sustainability bonds** [N2-R3]. This suggests that financial support is being structured around performance, accountability, and alignment with broader sustainability goals.

### 2.3 Land, housing, and urban planning signals

The land and urban planning signals are equally important. The housing-rebalancing source notes that **land-use rights revenue dropped by over 50% between 2021 and 2025**, and that local governments face **financial obligations to subsidize housing** [N1-R1]. The same source indicates that the new development model demands a transition away from one-off fiscal windfalls toward more sustainable revenue sources, including a broader local tax base, reforms to **central-local revenue sharing**, and, over the longer term, new recurrent sources of local revenue such as a **property tax** [N1-F1].

The land-supply-reform literature suggests that **supply-side structural reform of the land market** can help integrate land, capital, and labor factors and increase effective supply [N5-R4]. It also notes that improving the efficiency of the supply of developable land is more effective than simply increasing allocations of land for residential development [N5-R5]. The urban-planning context also shows that authorities have issued various policies and regulations on **land use, environmental management, and related areas** in response to the pandemic [N1-R2].

Taken together, these signals suggest a future in which real estate development will be shaped by **more efficient land use, more sustainable local revenue arrangements, and more integrated urban planning** [N1-R2][N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 3) Structural constraints and reform paths limiting or reshaping real estate growth

The structural constraints are mainly **housing supply and land availability bottlenecks, financial viability and financing constraints, and the need for more stable development conditions through land and housing reforms**.

### 3.1 Housing supply and land availability bottlenecks

The evidence is very strong on supply-side constraints. The housing-rebalancing source notes that China’s property downturn has lasted five years and that declining property values have impaired household, developer, and local government balance sheets [N1-F1]. It also states that **land-use rights revenue dropped by over 50% between 2021 and 2025**, and that local governments face **financial obligations to subsidize housing** [N1-R1]. The land-supply-reform literature argues that current Chinese national government policies are **insufficient to resolve urban housing shortfalls**, that demand for affordable housing far outstrips supply, and that **limits on land allocation for villas increase competition for regular commodity housing** [N5-F4]. It further notes that competition for regular commodity housing decreases access for moderate-income households and that improving the efficiency of the supply of developable land is more effective than simply increasing allocations of land for residential development [N5-F4][N5-R5].

The urbanization literature adds that China’s urban populations are expected to expand by **255 million by 2050**, intensifying urban housing shortfalls [N5-F4]. So the main constraint is not merely a shortage of land, but an inefficient land-use system that creates mismatched supply relative to demand [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F4][N5-R5].

### 3.2 Financial viability and financing constraints

It also states that local governments have been selling land-use rights to cover expenditure gaps and supplement infrastructure funding, and that the new development model demands a transition away from one-off fiscal windfalls toward more sustainable revenue sources [N1-F1]. The land-supply-reform source notes that **supply-side structural reform of the land market helps integrate land, capital, and labor factors and increase effective supply** [N5-R4]. The same source also argues that improving the efficiency of the supply of developable land is more effective than simply increasing allocations of land for residential development [N5-R5]. These sources together indicate that developers and local governments face serious financing constraints, partly because land sales are no longer sufficient to fund local spending, and partly because residential land markets are inefficient [N5-R1][N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R5].

### 3.3 How land and housing reforms can create more stable development conditions

The reform path is positive but conditional. The land-supply-reform literature proposes a **dynamic model for reform** and advocates partitioning residential land among housing classifications tied to target household sectors, including optimizing land supply for affordable housing, deregulating land supply for high-end commodity housing, and taxing high-end commodity housing [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a reform path in which land and housing reforms can stabilize development by making land use more efficient, expanding affordable housing supply, and reducing reliance on land-sale dependency [N5-F4][N1-F1][N5-R4].

## 4) Future risks, constraints, and structural changes that may limit or reshape real estate growth

The future risks and structural changes are significant, but the evidence is strongest on supply-side bottlenecks and less direct on demographic and demand-side pressures.

### 4.1 Demographic and demand-side pressures

The evidence is limited and indirect. The housing-rebalancing report notes that China’s property downturn has lasted five years and that declining property values have encouraged precautionary savings and dampened consumption [N1-F1]. It also states that housing remains the primary store of household wealth in China, and that declining property values have created a paradox between assertive top-level rhetoric and a restrained policy playbook [N1-F1]. This suggests that demand-side pressures are real and persistent, but the source does not provide a robust, decade-specific demographic forecast.

The urbanization literature adds that China’s urban populations are expected to expand by **255 million by 2050**, intensifying urban housing shortfalls [N5-F4]. However, this is presented as a background socioeconomic condition rather than a near-term demand-side constraint [N5-F4]. So the evidence supports the idea that demand-side pressures will remain a concern, especially through affordability and consumption-side effects, but it does not provide a robust, decade-specific demographic forecast [N1-F1][N5-F4].

### 4.2 Regulatory and enforcement risks in sustainability implementation

The evidence is mixed. On one hand, the green-finance literature indicates that regulators are tightening expectations on use-of-proceeds, impact indicators, and external review for labelled green and sustainability bonds [N2-R3]. This suggests that implementation risks are being addressed through stricter oversight. On the other hand, the climate-action source notes that China’s current policies scenario are rated as **“Insufficient”** when compared to their fair-share contribution to climate change mitigation [N1-F2]. It also notes that China’s climate policies and action need substantial improvements to be consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C, and that if all countries followed China’s approach, warming would reach over 2°C and up to 3°C [N1-F2]. This implies that enforcement risks and policy gaps may persist if China cannot accelerate its climate transition.

The housing-rebalancing source also indicates that local governments have been selling land-use rights to cover expenditure gaps and supplement infrastructure funding, and that the new development model demands a transition away from one-off fiscal windfalls toward more sustainable revenue sources [N1-F1]. While this is more about fiscal governance than direct sustainability enforcement, it still reflects the risk that weak implementation of new policy frameworks can undermine sustainability goals [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### 4.3 How urbanization slowdown and ESG demands will change development models

The evidence points to a structural shift toward affordability, livability, and decarbonization. The new property development model is described as shifting housing away from its role as a primary wealth accumulation vehicle toward its social function as shelter, by incrementally increasing the share of affordable housing in new supply and steering the market toward greater price stability [N1-F1]. The land-supply-reform literature argues that current Chinese national government policies are insufficient to resolve urban housing shortfalls, that demand for affordable housing far outstrips supply, and that reforms should integrate housing provision across affordable and commodity sectors [N5-F4]. It also suggests that deregulation of land supply for and taxation of high-end commodity housing can ease housing stress [N5-F4].

At the same time, the energy-transition excerpt shows that China’s rapid renewables rollout is the main driver of decarbonisation and that the NDRC’s draft implementation measures are shifting from supply-side incentives to demand-side obligations [N1-F2]. This indicates that future development models will be more focused on **sustainable energy systems, affordable housing, and integrated land-use planning** rather than on speculative price growth [N1-F1][N5-F4][N1-F2]. The comparative policy-context evidence also notes that China uses a **planning-driven model focused on national goals and technical standards**, which is consistent with a more controlled, technical, and long-term development model [N4-R1].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

### What is the core driver of sustainable real estate development?

The core driver is **policy and regulatory pressure**. Green building standards, land-use regulation, and climate-energy transition policy are the main levers [N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-R2][N1-F2]. Market and investor behavior support green development, but the evidence is less direct [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. Technical and operational improvements are strongest in energy efficiency and renewables [N1-F2], but material-use details are thinner [N4-R1].

### What is the likely future policy direction?

The state is likely to support real estate development through a combination of **financial easing, green finance, ESG capital, affordability measures, fiscal governance reform, land-use regulation, and supply-side land reform** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F3][N2-R3][N1-R2][N1-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The emphasis will be on **stabilization, affordability, fiscal sustainability, and structural rebalancing** rather than cyclical stimulus [N1-F1].

### What structural constraints must be addressed?

The main structural constraints are **housing supply and land availability bottlenecks** and **financial viability and financing constraints** [N1-F1][N1-R1][N5-F4][N5-R5]. Land and housing reforms can create more stable development conditions by improving land-use efficiency, expanding affordable housing, and reducing reliance on land-sale dependency [N5-F4][N1-F1][N5-R4].

### What are the key risks?

The key risks are **persistent affordability and fiscal constraints**, potential **enforcement gaps in sustainability implementation**, and the possibility that regulatory looseness may not be sufficient to stabilize demand [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. At the same time, **urbanization slowdown and ESG demands** will reshape development models toward affordability, livability, and decarbonization [N1-F1][N5-F4][N1-F2].

## 6) Bottom line

In short, China’s real estate industry is moving from a **growth-driven model** toward a **sustainable, balanced, and socially oriented model**. The future will depend on:  
- **stronger green building and energy-policy frameworks** [N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-F2];  
- **a more mature green finance and ESG capital market** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F3];  
- **efficient land-use reform and urban planning** [N1-R2][N1-R1][N5-R4];  
- **affordable housing and fiscal sustainability** [N1-F1][N5-F4];  
- **a shift toward livability, price stability, and decarbonization** [N1-F1][N5-F4][N1-F2].

The evidence supports a cautious but optimistic conclusion: the industry can be made more sustainable and orderly, but only if policy, finance, and land reforms are pursued in tandem and with sufficient attention to implementation and enforcement [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R3][N5-F4].
